extracted.intended_audience: General readers, fans and researchers of British comedy and television
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria relevant to producing or evaluating a British satirical panel/talk show that mixes stand-up, debated propositions, guest discussion and monologues (as exemplified by Frankie Boyle's New World Order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall episode structure
rubrics_metrics.description: After a few minutes of stand-up, he makes two statements and discusses them with his guests. Boyle summarises each debate in a short monologue to camera. The programme finishes with Boyle sitting against the desk delivering a final longer monologue to camera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines a clear three-part episode flow: short stand-up intro, guest discussion of two propositions with short summaries, and a closing longer monologue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of provocative propositions as prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes list 'Propositions discussed' (e.g. 'The Political System Hates Us', 'Donald Trump Will Save The World').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmes anchor discussion around bold, provocative thesis statements to generate debate and comedic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular and rotating guest roster / diversity of guests
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout its six series, regular guests included Sara Pascoe, Katherine Ryan, Mona Chalabi, Miles Jupp, Sophie Duker and Kiri Pritchard-McLean. The show used a 'diverse roster of rotating guests', including guest lineups that were entirely female or non-white, and gave opportunities to lesser-known comedians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A varied mix of regulars and rotating guests (including underrepresented voices) is part of the show's identity and is noted positively in reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of subject-matter contributors (e.g., data journalist)
rubrics_metrics.description: The data journalist Mona Chalabi became a regular in series two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bringing in specialists (e.g., data journalists) can broaden content beyond pure comedy and add informational or analytical angles to discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshopping and rehearsal process
rubrics_metrics.description: Boyle said he would workshop material for the series in the Glee Club, Glasgow from July to the recording—this includes the closing monologues. He planned around 40 'warm-up shows' to practice jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive live warm-up and workshopping is used to refine material, particularly monologues and punchlines, before recording for broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening material strategy ('three big jokes')
rubrics_metrics.description: Boyle said: 'there's often a bit at the start where there's three big jokes that lead you in', to 'try and get [the audience] on board and create some confidence with them'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structuring the opening with several strong jokes builds audience rapport and sets the tone for the episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode running time and special lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Running time: 30 minutes (Election special 40 minutes, Review of the year specials 45 minutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard episodes are half-hour; allow extended duration for election/review specials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format adaptations for production circumstances (e.g., COVID-19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Series 4 was filmed without a studio audience, with a revised socially-distanced set due to COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production must adapt set and audience arrangements in response to external constraints while retaining show format where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual/year-in-review specials
rubrics_metrics.description: The show had annual specials that review news of the year (e.g., 'Frankie Boyle's 2017 New World Order', review shows in subsequent years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including end-of-year review specials is a recurring format choice to summarise and satirise the year's events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political stance and editorial tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The Independent's Louis Chilton deemed the show 'one of the few shows on TV that was sincerely and unapologetically left-wing', with criticisms of Keir Starmer and tacit agreement for revolution; centrist guests could also air their views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An overt political stance can define the show's identity but may influence audience composition, critical reception and broadcaster relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of viewership trends and broadcaster priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer for Chortle commented that the BBC was potentially shifting prioritisation away from panel shows and towards scripted comedy, and that New World Order's viewership had declined over time. The show was cancelled on 23 March 2023.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcaster programming decisions and audience figures are practical criteria that affect a show's continuation regardless of creative quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical recognition / awards
rubrics_metrics.description: The show was nominated for the best Entertainment Performance BAFTA in 2020.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry nominations and awards are measures of critical recognition and can be used to evaluate a show's impact and quality.
